dedupe_keys.name: hurricane harvey household survey of utility disruptions in houston and diim economic losses

description: This case study measures how electricity, water, phone, internet, public transport, workplaces and grocery stores in Houston performed during Hurricane Harvey in 2017 and turns the disruptions into economic losses. Shahnawaz Rafi, Sisi Meng, Joost Santos and Pallab Mozumder surveyed 500 residents of the Houston metropolitan area after landfall and published the study in Economics of Disasters and Climate Change in December 2023. About 70 percent of households lost electricity, 51 percent had no water for up to six days, two-thirds lacked internet, half lost phone service, 71 percent could not commute and 73 percent could not buy groceries. Feeding these disruption shares and durations into the Dynamic Inoperability Input-Output Model gave losses of US$6.7 to 9.7 billion across interconnected sectors. Coverage is the Houston metropolitan area. Format and access: a journal article with an open preprint; the survey microdata are not released. Licence: preprint CC-BY; article terms not read. Caveats: survey recall and sample size limit precision, and losses depend on assumed working days. It gives disruption durations for cascading failure and resilience models of hurricanes. Related catalogue records are the Harvey, Irma and Maria supply chain observations and the Hurricane Harvey food access survey.
